name: Times Literary Supplement cryptic crossword No 1,175

solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: A form of examination including T-cell?

indicators.note: to include something is to take it inside, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: to peer is to look closely, one way of examining
the letter taken as printed

explanation.surface: A medical test that looks for T-cells in the blood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'T-cell' reads as one immunology term, but the hyphen splits it: T is wordplay and 'cell' is the definition. PEER with T inside gives PETER.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter is old criminal slang for a prison cell, and also for a safe.

clue.text: Criticize 1A who’s immature

blocks.note: first meaning: to review harshly
second meaning: J M Barrie's boy who never grows up, whose first name is the answer to 1 across

explanation.walkthrough: 1A is PETER, and the boy who refuses to grow up is Peter PAN, so the cross-reference supplies the missing half of his name.
explanation.definitionFit: To pan a play or book is to give it a scathing review; Barrie's eternal child is surnamed Pan.

clue.text: What comes before the end of the morning, in Frayn’s story including newspaper crosswords

definitions.text: What comes before the end of the morning, in Frayn’s story including newspaper crosswords

blocks.clueFragment: What comes before the end of the morning
blocks.note: surface reading: some event that happens shortly before noon

blocks.clueFragment: in Frayn’s story including newspaper crosswords
blocks.note: setter's reading: the first word of the title of Michael Frayn's Fleet Street novel, which features a crossword compiler

explanation.surface: Something that happens late in the morning in a Michael Frayn tale about a newspaper office.
explanation.walkthrough: Michael Frayn's 1967 novel is 'Towards the End of the Morning', set on a Fleet Street paper; the word literally comes before 'the End of the Morning' in its title.
explanation.definitionFit: The preposition opens the novel's title, so it is literally the word placed ahead of the rest of that title.

clue.text: A 1A who loses his jacket and shoes after stealing some food

definitions.text: A 1A who loses his jacket and shoes after stealing some food

blocks.clueFragment: A 1A who loses his jacket and shoes
blocks.note: surface reading: some man named Peter who gets robbed of his clothes
setter's reading: Beatrix Potter's naughty character, who raids Mr McGregor's vegetable garden and leaves his blue jacket and shoes behind

explanation.surface: A thief called Peter loses his coat and shoes after a petty theft of food.
explanation.walkthrough: 1A is PETER; in Beatrix Potter's tale Peter Rabbit steals lettuces and radishes, then loses his jacket and shoes escaping from the gardener.
explanation.definitionFit: Beatrix Potter's most famous character is a young bunny called Peter, whose surname is his species.

clue.text: Pa and I had curious elegy from Edmund on the death of a daughter

definitions.text: elegy from Edmund on the death of a daughter

indicators.note: something curious is odd or strange, so the letters come out in an odd order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A father and his child shared a strange poem of mourning by someone named Edmund about a lost daughter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Edmund' is Edmund Spenser; 'Pa and I had' supplies every letter once.
explanation.definitionFit: Spenser's 1591 elegy mourns Douglas Howard, daughter of Lord Howard and wife of Arthur Gorges, who died young.

clue.text: Wipe, like wipe? That’s not very interesting

blocks.note: to wipe dishes is to dry them
like and as both mean in the manner of
to wipe a shelf is to dust it

explanation.surface: Someone complaining that housework, all that wiping, is tedious.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated 'wipe' looks like padding, but it gives two different synonyms. Dr Dryasdust is a fictional pedant in Scott's prefaces, hence the word for dull scholarship.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes something dull, dry and pedantic, especially tedious scholarly writing that holds no reader's attention.

clue.text: Cup is reshaped for an ancient monarch

indicators.note: reshaping something gives it a new form, so these letters take a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written; it also serves the indicator phrase

explanation.surface: A trophy is remade for an old king's use.
explanation.walkthrough: Picus was a legendary early king of Latium, turned into a woodpecker by Circe for rejecting her.
explanation.definitionFit: In Roman legend Picus ruled Latium long before Rome, so he counts as a monarch of antiquity.

clue.text: Christie’s spy mystery, with a chap somewhere in Northern France

blocks.note: Agatha Christie's wartime spy novel is titled 'N or M?'
a man's name standing for any chap

explanation.surface: An Agatha Christie espionage novel set somewhere in the north of France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'N or M?' is a 1941 Tommy and Tuppence novel; read without spaces or punctuation its title gives four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The region is a historic province on the northern French coast, famous for the 1944 landings.

clue.text: Anger and trouble for a Shakespeare faker

indicators.note: to trouble something is to disturb it, so the letters are stirred into another order

blocks.note: to rile someone is to anger them
taken as written

explanation.surface: Fury and difficulty await a man who forges Shakespeare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Anger and trouble' reads as two nouns, but 'Anger' is a verb meaning rile and 'trouble' is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: William Henry Ireland forged Shakespeare documents and the play Vortigern in the 1790s before confessing the fraud.

clue.text: Detective story, with a railway station as Sir Humphrey’s objective

blocks.note: Sir Humphrey Appleby is the scheming civil servant in the TV comedy Yes, Minister
an objective is an end one aims at

explanation.surface: A crime novel in which a train station is the goal of a senior civil servant.
explanation.walkthrough: Michael Innes's 1945 novel sends his detective John Appleby to a station called Appleby's End, so the railway station is a fair extra hint.
explanation.definitionFit: The title is one of Michael Innes's Inspector Appleby mysteries, a classic piece of Golden Age crime fiction.

clue.text: One delivering stories daily?

blocks.note: surface reading: a storyteller or author who produces tales
setter's reading: the stories are newspaper reports and the daily is a paper brought round each morning

explanation.walkthrough: 'Delivering stories' suggests a writer, but the delivery is a paper round and the stories are those in the daily paper.
explanation.definitionFit: A lad who carries newspapers door to door, or sells them on the street, brings the day's reports to readers.

clue.text: Coe’s best-known achievement involved this dodgy sporting arrangement

blocks.note: first meaning: Jonathan Coe's best-known novel, a 1994 satire of Thatcher-era Britain, has an exclamation for a title built around this word
second meaning: a crooked fix in which a result or spoils are shared out in advance

explanation.surface: Sebastian Coe's great athletic triumph turns out to have been a fix.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coe' and 'sporting' point to the Olympic runner Sebastian Coe, but this is the novelist Jonathan Coe, whose 1994 satire is 'What a Carve Up!'
explanation.definitionFit: A carve-up is an underhand sharing out or fixing of an outcome, as in a rigged race or match.

clue.text: A chap’s adventure that isn’t by P G Wodehouse, but is about a pig

definitions.text: A chap’s adventure that isn’t by P G Wodehouse, but is about a pig

blocks.clueFragment: A chap’s adventure that isn’t by P G Wodehouse
blocks.note: surface reading: a scrape of the kind Bertie Wooster gets into, yet not from Wodehouse's pen
setter's reading: Kenneth Grahame's short tale whose hero is a pig named after a man

explanation.surface: A comic story about a young man's scrape that sounds like Wodehouse but is really about a pig.
explanation.walkthrough: Wodehouse brings Bertie Wooster to mind, and his Lord Emsworth's pig too, but this is Kenneth Grahame's story of Bertie the pig, published in 1949.
explanation.definitionFit: Kenneth Grahame's story follows a pig who sneaks out on a moonlit jaunt, so the title names a pig's adventure.

clue.text: Roger the conjuror, destroyed by diabolical goblin

indicators.note: something diabolical is devilishly wrong, so the letters are thrown out of their order

blocks.note: taken as written
something broke is wrecked or destroyed

explanation.surface: A stage magician called Roger is ruined by a wicked goblin.
explanation.walkthrough: Roger Bolingbroke is the conjurer who raises a spirit for the Duchess of Gloucester in Shakespeare's Henry VI Part 2.
explanation.definitionFit: Roger Bolingbroke was a real fifteenth-century astrologer executed for sorcery, dramatised by Shakespeare as a conjurer.

clue.text: Most unlikely to be Mary Shelley’s kind of man

blocks.note: first meaning: the least probable, as in 'the final person you would expect'
second meaning: the title of Mary Shelley's 1826 novel about the sole survivor of a plague that ends humanity

explanation.surface: Someone who would never become the sort of man Mary Shelley wrote about.
explanation.walkthrough: Mary Shelley brings Frankenstein's creature to mind, but the man meant is the title figure of her later novel 'The Last Man'.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means least probable, as in 'the final person one would ask'; Shelley's novel titles its hero by that word.

clue.text: Sweet parent, or someone less charming?

blocks.note: sugar is what makes things sweet, and a term of endearment
a familiar word for a father

explanation.surface: A loving father, or else a figure with rather less appeal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet parent' reads as a fond description, but it builds the phrase literally; the definition hints that he is no Prince Charming.
explanation.definitionFit: A sugar daddy is a rich older man who lavishes gifts on a younger lover; his appeal lies in money rather than charm.

clue.text: With protection like this, he killed a king

blocks.note: an aegis is a shield or protection, originally that of Zeus and Athena
thus means in this way, like this

explanation.surface: An assassin explains how he was shielded when he murdered a monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth Aegisthus, lover of Clytemnestra, helped murder Agamemnon on his return from Troy.
explanation.definitionFit: Aegisthus killed Agamemnon, king of Mycenae, and also his own uncle Atreus, so he is a royal murderer twice over.

clue.text: One presiding over trees gives a kind of birch without hesitation to a group of students

indicators.note: without means lacking, so something is left out of the word before it

blocks.note: the silver birch is a common species
er is the sound of hesitating
taken as written
the NUS is Britain's National Union of Students

explanation.surface: A forest overseer hands a birch tree to a student union.
explanation.walkthrough: Silvanus was the Roman god of woods and fields; the NUS is the UK's national student union.
explanation.definitionFit: Silvanus is the Roman deity of forests and uncultivated land, so he is a divine guardian presiding over woodland.

clue.text: Cheap wine – inn gave ton away

indicators.note: to give something away is to let it go astray, so these letters wander out of order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A pub serves plonk and gives away a huge quantity of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ton' looks like a weight being removed, but nothing is subtracted: all ten letters of 'inn gave ton' are used.
explanation.definitionFit: Wine without a stated year is a blend of harvests, usually the more ordinary and inexpensive bottles.

clue.text: Nothing to do with the ears of East African people

definitions.note: adjective: relating to the peoples of the Nile region

blocks.note: nil is zero, nothing
otic is the medical adjective for the ear

explanation.surface: A remark that some East African peoples have no connection with hearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nothing to do with' reads as one idiom, but 'Nothing' and 'to do with the ears' are separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Nilotic peoples, such as the Maasai, Luo and Dinka, live along the upper Nile valley in East Africa.

clue.text: Colour, first seen with 1A in black and white

definitions.text: first seen with 1A in black and white

blocks.note: first meaning: the colour of the sky

blocks.clueFragment: first seen with 1A in black and white
blocks.note: second meaning: the first word of the BBC children's programme named with 1 across, which began on black-and-white television in 1958

explanation.walkthrough: 1A is PETER; Blue Peter is a long-running British children's TV show, first broadcast before colour television.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a primary colour and also precedes Peter in the programme's title, a nice irony for a monochrome broadcast.

clue.text: Singles falling in love again, she gave us

indicators.note: falling things tumble and land in disorder, so the letters drop into a new sequence

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Unattached people falling in love once more, thanks to her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Falling in love' is one phrase on the surface; cryptically 'falling' is the signal and 'love again' belongs to the definition, as Doris Lessing's 1996 novel is 'Love, Again'.
explanation.definitionFit: Doris Lessing, the Nobel laureate, wrote the late novel titled Love, Again, so she is its author.

clue.text: It was used to comb Sir 1A in a comedy of manners

definitions.text: Sir 1A in a comedy of manners

blocks.note: first meaning: the spiky dried flower head used to raise the nap on cloth, an old spelling of teasel

blocks.clueFragment: Sir 1A in a comedy of manners
blocks.note: second meaning: Sir Peter, the elderly husband in Sheridan's The School for Scandal

explanation.surface: Something used to tidy the hair of a knight in a Restoration-style comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 1A is PETER: Sir Peter Teazle is the old husband in Sheridan's 'The School for Scandal'. The plant's spiny heads were used to tease cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: Teazle is a variant spelling of teasel, a thistle-like plant whose prickly heads fullers used to card woollen fabric.

clue.text: Winner lost Hope in this story, but through the alternative to Charity, had …

definitions.text: Winner lost Hope in this story, but through the alternative to Charity, had …

blocks.clueFragment: Winner lost Hope in this story
blocks.note: surface reading: a victor who gave up hope, as if despairing despite winning

blocks.clueFragment: but through the alternative to Charity, had …
blocks.note: setter's reading: Arthur Winner is the hero of James Gould Cozzens's 1957 novel, and in 1 Corinthians 13 the word rendered charity is also translated as love

explanation.surface: A champion abandoned hope, yet thanks to a virtue was overcome by something.
explanation.walkthrough: Hope and Charity suggest the three virtues, but 'Winner' is Arthur Winner of Cozzens's novel, and the trailing dots run on into the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cozzens bestseller tells how its lawyer hero is driven and gripped by passion, reflected in the title.

clue.text: It’s mainly Basil and Oscar chasing a nuisance

indicators.note: to chase is to follow behind, so the piece named first goes after the one named second

blocks.note: a pest is an annoying nuisance
Oscar is O in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Two men, Basil and Oscar, pursue someone irritating.
explanation.walkthrough: Capitalised 'Basil' poses as a man's name beside Oscar, but it is the herb.
explanation.definitionFit: Pesto is a Genoese sauce whose chief ingredient is pounded basil leaves, with pine nuts, garlic, cheese and oil.

clue.text: … perverse gusto in excursions

indicators.note: perverse means contrary or turned the wrong way, so the letters are set awry

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: someone gripped by a twisted relish for trips.
explanation.walkthrough: The leading dots join this to 21 across for the surface only; the clue stands alone cryptically.
explanation.definitionFit: Outings and excursions are both short trips taken for pleasure, such as day trips to the seaside.

clue.text: Critic’s reported description of the TLS

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so it is the sound that counts

blocks.note: the TLS is the Times Literary Supplement, a paper that has literature, or lit, in it

explanation.surface: A reviewer's spoken account of what the Times Literary Supplement is like.
explanation.walkthrough: The TLS is the Times Literary Supplement, which publishes this puzzle; 'lit' is the casual short form of literature.
explanation.definitionFit: William Hazlitt was a celebrated Romantic essayist and critic of drama, painting and literature.

clue.text: Toni Morrison’s baby, not entirely proletarian?

indicators.note: taking a word not entirely means using only part of it, so the letters sit inside

blocks.note: the middle letters of the word

explanation.surface: A wry question whether Toni Morrison's child was only partly working class.
explanation.walkthrough: Toni Morrison's 1981 novel is 'Tar Baby', so her baby is the word before it; a tar is also a sailor, a working man, which colours the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The word that precedes Baby in the title of Morrison's novel is the one that names her baby here.

clue.text: Removed passages from journeys, with Italy replacing home of ancient civilization

indicators.note: replacing means taking the place of, so one letter group is swapped out for another

blocks.note: excursions are trips or journeys
I is the international vehicle code for Italy
Ur was a Sumerian city in Mesopotamia

explanation.surface: An editor cut sections from travel writing, replacing an ancient setting with Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sumerian city Ur is the 'home of ancient civilization'; I takes its place in the middle of the trips.
explanation.definitionFit: Excisions are cuts, especially passages deleted from a text by an editor or censor.

clue.text: Edmund’s half-brother, apparently mad, raged wildly

indicators.note: acting wildly means without control, so the letters run riot into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A man who seemed insane stormed about in a fury.
explanation.walkthrough: In King Lear, Edgar is Gloucester's legitimate son and Edmund's half-brother; he disguises himself as the madman Poor Tom.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Edgar feigns madness as Poor Tom on the heath, so he only seems to have lost his wits.
